title: CPU Performance: Clock Speed, Cache and Cores
intro: A short, self-paced catch-up covering the essential lesson ideas. Check every question, then correct anything missed.

stages.label: Remember
stages.lead: Retrieve two ideas from earlier learning.

options: Address of the location being accessed
questions.answer: Address of the location being accessed
questions.feedback: The Memory Address Register identifies which location is being accessed.

questions.prompt: Which kind of memory holds programs and data currently in use?
questions.feedback: RAM provides working memory for programs and data in use.

stages.label: Learn
stages.lead: Read the key concepts, visual model and worked explanation.

blocks.title: Clock speed
blocks.text: Clock speed is measured in Hz: clock cycles per second. One cycle does not necessarily equal one instruction.

blocks.title: Cache size
blocks.text: Cache stores frequently needed information closer to the CPU, reducing time spent accessing RAM.

blocks.title: Core count
blocks.text: Multiple cores enable more work in parallel when software supports simultaneous tasks.

blocks.title: Overall comparison
blocks.text: Architecture and task type also affect performance; do not infer an absolute winner from one specification.

blocks.title: Visual model · CPU Performance: Clock Speed, Cache and Cores
blocks.caption: The software workload and processor architecture also matter.

blocks.title: Worked example · Compare CPU A (2 GHz, 4 cores, 4 MB cache) with B (3 GHz, 2 cores, 8 MB cache). Which is faster?
blocks.text: CPU B has the higher clock speed. CPU A has more cores, which can help with suitably parallel work. CPU B has more cache, potentially reducing RAM access. Explain that workload and architecture determine real performance. Conclude neither is automatically fastest for every task.

items: clock speed — Number of CPU clock cycles per second.
cache — Small, fast memory holding frequently used information.
core — CPU processing unit able to execute instructions.
parallel processing — Running work simultaneously using multiple processing units.

questions.prompt: What does CPU clock speed measure?
questions.feedback: Clock speed is measured in hertz, with 1 GHz meaning one billion cycles per second.

questions.prompt: Why might more CPU cores improve performance?
options: They can run tasks in parallel when software supports it
questions.answer: They can run tasks in parallel when software supports it
questions.feedback: Parallel workloads may use more cores, unlike a single-threaded task.

options: Fast access to frequently used data
It increases the number of HDD platters
questions.answer: Fast access to frequently used data
questions.feedback: Cache reduces time spent waiting for slower RAM accesses.

blocks.text: Two CPUs both run at 2 GHz but one has twice as many cores. Explain why it may not always finish a task faster. [4 marks]

questions.prompt: The code prints clockGHz * seconds with 3 and 2. What prints?
After seconds changes from 2 to 4, what prints?
Why doesn't 3 GHz guarantee three billion instructions executed per second?
options: Instructions can take differing numbers of cycles
Every CPU always has one core
questions.answer: Instructions can take differing numbers of cycles
questions.feedback: Clock cycles are not identical to executed instructions.

writing.prompt: Two CPUs both run at 2 GHz but one has twice as many cores. Explain why it may not always finish a task faster. [4 marks]
writing.model: More parallel capacity [1]; only when software uses multiple threads [1]; single-threaded code cannot fully use extra cores [1]; other factors such as cache and architecture matter [1].
checklist: I explained how multiple cores can provide parallel processing.
I explained why a single-threaded task may not benefit.
I mentioned other factors such as cache, clock speed or architecture.
